newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Labour should not be under WTO 'at all' - G15.
newsitem.headline: Labour should not be under WTO 'at all' - G15.

text.p: The Group of 15 (G15) developing nations believe labour standards should not be in the programme of the World Trade Organisation (WTO) at all, Malaysian Trade Minister Rafidah Aziz said on Monday.
Speaking to reporters after a G15 meeting, she said: "We are all agreed that we don't want that (labour) to be discussed in WTO, and it should not come under the WTO's programme at all."

The United States is pushing hard for international trade rules to raise Third World labour standards, eradicate sweat shops and stop an estimated 250 million children working, and wants the WTO ministerial meeting in Singapore this week to move on the issue.
But many developing countries say the proposal is a protectionist ploy, and argue that both their economies and their workers would be worse off with such rules.
Some of them as well as several developed countries like Japan also say the appropriate place to consider the issue is the International Labour Organisation, not the WTO.

Rafidah said the G15 meeting had not discussed another major topic, an Information Technology Agreement (ITA) that would scrap tariffs on an estimated $1 trillion worth of annual world trade in computer and telecommunications products.
She noted, however, that Malaysia supports an ITA, but with flexibility allowing countries to go beyond a year 2000 target in making cuts.
"We subscribe to move towards having an ITA which will see substantial tariff cuts, but with the flexibility given to countries" on product coverage and a time frame.

On the question of government procurement, she said: "While we do believe there should be transparency in the government procurement practices...we don't want to see anything that impinges upon on national policies of members."
Europe and others at the WTO are advocating liberalisation of government procurement policies.
